links.note: 541 defines முறை (justice) as inquiring (ஓர்ந்து), favouring no one (கண்ணோடாது) and acting after deliberation (தேர்ந்து செய்வது). 561 repeats the inquiry (தக்காங்கு நாடி) and adds two things 541 leaves unsaid: the penalty must match the offence (ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது) and its aim is that the wrong not go further (தலைச்செல்லா வண்ணத்தால்). Read together, the chapter on not terrorising opens by restating the rule of justice with a limit on punishment built in.

561 makes the king the one who punishes in proportion (ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது வேந்து), while 579 calls it the highest quality to show kindly regard and bear with even those whose way is to hurt (ஒறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பினார் கண்ணும் ... பொறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பே தலை). The same root ஒறு sits on opposite sides. Parimelazhagar separates the cases: 561 concerns wrongs done to weaker subjects, 579 wrongs done to the ruler himself, so forbearance is limited to injuries that are the ruler's own to forgive.

562 tells those who want lasting prosperity to raise the rod sharply but strike gently (கடிதோச்சி மெல்ல எறிக). 567 names what happens when the stroke is not gentle: punishment past the bound (கையிகந்த தண்டம்), with harsh words, is a file that wears down the king's strength. 562 gives the practice and 567 the cost of abandoning it; the 'long prosperity' (நெடிதாக்கம்) of one is the 'conquering strength' (அடுமுரண்) eroded in the other.

562 asks for a light stroke after a stern show (மெல்ல எறிக); Manakkudavar takes this to mean the penalty should fall short of what the offence deserves. 550 says a king's punishing the cruel with death (கொலையிற் கொடியாரை வேந்தொறுத்தல்) is like weeding the young crop. The pairing marks where gentleness stops: for those 550 calls கொடியார், the book accepts the severest penalty.

563 says a cruel-sceptred king who keeps doing what terrifies (வெருவந்த செய்தொழுகும் வெங்கோலன்) will certainly and quickly perish (ஒருவந்தம் ஒல்லைக் கெடும்). 548 says a king who is not easy of access and does not inquire and do justice will sink and perish of himself (தானே கெடும்). Neither verse needs an enemy to bring the king down: in both the misrule is itself the cause of the fall.

564 says the king of whom the painful words 'our lord is harsh' (இறைகடியன் என்றுரைக்கும் இன்னாச்சொல்) are spoken will quickly perish. 555 says the tears of those who cannot bear their affliction are the weapon that wears away wealth (செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும் படை). In both, what destroys the ruler comes from the subjects' suffering, as speech in one verse and as tears in the other.

386 says that if a king is easy to see and not harsh of speech, his land is spoken of above others (மீக்கூறும் மன்னன் நிலம்). 564 gives the reverse case: where people say 'our lord is harsh' (இறைகடியன்), the king quickly perishes. Both verses measure a reign by what is said about it.

386 praises the king who is easy to see (காட்சிக்கு எளியன்) and not harsh of speech. 565 describes his opposite, hard to get an audience with (அருஞ்செவ்வி) and grim of face (இன்னா முகத்தான்), and says his great wealth is as if a demon had seen it (பேஎய்கண் டன்னது). The ideal of the opening chapter on kingship returns here in the negative, with its cost stated.

565 says the great wealth (பெருஞ்செல்வம்) of an inaccessible, grim-faced man is as if seen by a demon; Parimelazhagar explains that no one approaches him, so the wealth is of use neither to him nor to others. 1000 says the great wealth (பெருஞ்செல்வம்) gained by one without courtesy (பண்பிலான்) is like good milk spoiled by its vessel. Outside the court the same judgment holds: the holder's manner ruins wealth that is sound in itself.

566 says that if the ruler is harsh of speech and 'eyeless' (கண்ணிலன்), his long-standing wealth perishes at once; Parimelazhagar takes கண் here to stand for கண்ணோட்டம். 577, in the next chapter, states the equation directly: those without kindly regard have no eyes (கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லவர் கண்ணிலர்). The single word in 566 is the idea the following chapter spells out.

386 names not being harsh of speech (கடுஞ்சொல்லன் அல்லனேல்) as what makes a king's land praised. 566 uses the same word, கடுஞ்சொல்லன், for the ruler whose great wealth is lost on the spot (ஆங்கே கெடும்). The quality is stated as a merit in the chapter on a king's excellence and as a cause of ruin here.

567 calls harsh words and excessive punishment a file (அரம்) that wears down (தேய்க்கும்) the king's conquering strength. 888 says a family with enmity inside it wears away (தேயும்) like metal rubbed by a file (அரம்பொருத பொன்போல), its strength ground down. In both the file stands for slow loss of strength from within, by the king's own conduct in one and by a house's own members in the other.

555 calls the tears of the afflicted the weapon that wears away wealth (செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும் படை); 567 calls harsh words and punishment beyond bounds the file that wears away the king's strength (அடுமுரண் தேய்க்கும் அரம்). Both use the verb தேய் with a tool: the adjoining chapters on misrule picture a tyrant's ruin as abrasion, not as a single blow.

462 says nothing is out of reach for those who act after examining a matter with chosen company and thinking it through (தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணி). 568 says the fortune of a king who does not think with his circle (இனத்தாற்றி எண்ணாத) and then rages in anger will shrink. The same pair of words, இனம் and எண்ணுதல், gives the rule in one verse and the failure in the other.

306 says anger, the fire that kills what it touches, burns even the safe raft called one's people (இனமென்னும் ஏமப் புணையைச் சுடும்). 568 shows this at court: the king who neglects his circle (இனம்) and then turns his anger on them (சினத்தாற்றிச் சீறின்) loses his fortune; Parimelazhagar adds that the frightened ministers leave him. The general warning in the book of virtue becomes a specific danger for a ruler.

569 says a king who has made no defence (சிறைசெய்யா வேந்தன்) will be seized by fear when war comes and quickly perish. 534 says that for the fearful there is no fort (அச்ச முடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை); Parimelazhagar explains that defences are no use to a frightened mind. One verse says lack of a fort produces fear, the other that fear cancels a fort, so the fort is necessary but not sufficient.

435 says the life of one who does not guard before a fault arrives (வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான்) perishes like straw before fire. 569 applies the same logic to war: the king who has not prepared his defence beforehand is overtaken when the battle arrives (செருவந்த போழ்தில்) and perishes. Both place the failure in the time before the danger, not in the moment of it.

570 says the harsh sceptre binds the unlearned to itself, and that the earth has no burden other than this (அதுவல்லது இல்லை நிலக்குப் பொறை). 572, two verses later, uses the same phrase for a different group: the mere existence of those without kindly regard is a burden to the earth (நிலக்குப் பொறை). The repeated phrase ties the last verse on tyranny to the chapter on kindly regard, though 570's 'no other burden' sits loosely beside 572 naming a second one.

447 asks who can ruin a ruler who keeps as his own those who will rebuke him (இடிக்குந் துணையாரை யாள்வாரை). 570 shows the opposite court: the harsh sceptre gathers the unlearned around it (கல்லார்ப் பிணிக்கும்), because, as Parimelazhagar says, such a ruler admits only those who will go along with him. The two verses together make a ruler's choice of companions a sign of the kind of rule he runs.

571 says this world exists because the great beauty called kindly regard exists (கண்ணோட்டம் ... உண்மையான் உண்டிவ் வுலகு). 996 says the world exists by resting on people of courtesy, and would otherwise sink into the earth and perish (பண்புடையார்ப் பட்டுண்டு உலகம்). Both use the same construction, உண்டு உலகு, to say that a human quality and not power keeps the world going; 571 says it in a chapter on kings and 996 of people in general.

557 says that a king's lack of tender care (அளியின்மை) is to those who live under him what lack of rain is to the earth. 571 states the positive side: the world exists because kindly regard exists; Parimelazhagar reads this of kings. In both verses the ruler's kindness is treated as a condition of life for the people, not as an ornament only.

572 says the existence of those without kindly regard is a burden to the earth (அஃதிலார் உண்மை நிலக்குப் பொறை). 1003 says the very appearance of men who cling to accumulation and do not want renown is a burden to the earth (தோற்றம் நிலக்குப் பொறை). The phrase is identical, and in both the people called a burden are those who are of no use to others.

983 lists kindly regard (கண்ணோட்டம்) with love, shame, obligingness and truth as the five pillars that hold up worth (சால்பு). 572 gives it a wider load: the conduct of the world rests in it (கண்ணோட்டத் துள்ளது உலகியல்). The quality that is one support of personal character in 983 is the support of social life in 572.

573 asks what use an eye is without kindly regard (கண்என்னாம் கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்), as a melody is no use that does not fit the song. 705 asks what use eyes are among the limbs if they cannot read another's sign (என்ன பயத்தவோ கண்). Both judge the eye by what it does for another person, kindness in one verse and understanding in the other, and not by sight.

79 asks what all the outer limbs can do for those who lack love, the inner limb (புறத்துறுப் பெல்லாம் எவன்செய்யும் ... அன்பிலவர்க்கு). 573 asks the same kind of question of the eye that lacks kindly regard. In both a visible organ is counted useless without the inner quality it should serve.

574 says eyes without kindly regard in due measure (அளவினால் கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்) do nothing but seem to be in the face; Parimelazhagar takes அளவினால் as excluding excessive indulgence. 578 says what the measure is: kindly regard shown without ruining the task (கருமம் சிதையாமல் கண்ணோட வல்லார்). The one word of limit in 574 becomes the whole subject of 578.

406 says the unlearned can only be said to exist (உளரென்னும் மாத்திரையர்) and are otherwise like barren saline land. 574 says eyes without kindly regard only seem to be there in the face (உளபோல் முகத்து) and do nothing more. Both verses grant bare existence and deny any use, of unlearned persons in one case and of unkind eyes in the other.

393 says only the learned are said to have eyes, and the unlearned have two sores on the face (முகத்திரண்டு புண்ணுடையர்). 575 says kindly regard is the eye's ornament and without it the eye is known for a sore (புண்ணென்று உணரப் படும்). The same image of the eye as a wound is used twice, once for lack of learning and once for lack of kindness, so the book gives the eye two conditions for being an eye.

1014 asks whether shame is not an ornament (அணி) to the worthy, and whether without it their proud walk is not a disease (அஃதின்றேல் பிணி). 575 has the same shape: kindly regard is the eye's ornament (அணிகலம்), and without it (அஃதின்றேல்) the eye is a sore (புண்). In both the missing virtue does not leave the thing plain but turns it into an affliction.

997 says those without human courtesy are like trees (மரம்போல்வர் மக்கட்பண்பு இல்லாதவர்), even if sharp as a file. 576 says those who have eyes and do not turn them kindly are like trees joined to the soil (மண்ணோ டியைந்த மரத்தனையர்). The tree is the book's figure for a person who lacks fellow-feeling, whatever else they have.

600 says those without inner drive are trees, and their human form is the only difference (மரம் மக்க ளாதலே வேறு). 576 says those who have eyes and do not extend kindly regard are like trees fixed in the earth. The same comparison is used for two different lacks, energy and kindness, so that both count as part of what makes someone a person.

Manakkudavar reads 576's மண்ணோ டியைந்த மரம் as a wooden doll finished with plaster, a reading Parimelazhagar mentions and rejects in favour of a living tree. On Manakkudavar's reading the verse joins 1020, where the movements of those with no shame within are like a wooden puppet (மரப்பாவை) feigning life by its string. The link holds only on that reading.

393 says those who are called 'people with eyes' are the learned (கண்ணுடையர் என்பவர் கற்றோர்). 577 says those without kindly regard are eyeless and those who have eyes do not lack it (கண்ணுடையார் கண்ணோட்டம் இன்மையும் இல்). The same title, கண்ணுடையார், is awarded on two different tests, learning and kindly regard; the verses do not conflict, but a reader should see that the book defines 'having eyes' twice.

541 makes it part of justice to show partiality to no one (யார்மாட்டும் கண்ணோடாது). 578 says the world belongs to those able to show kindly regard without ruining their task (கருமம் சிதையாமல் கண்ணோட வல்லார்க்கு); Parimelazhagar takes கருமம் as the work of doing justice and cites 541 himself. The two uses of கண்ணோடு set the boundary: kindness is praised up to the point where it would bend a judgment, and withheld there.

151 says bearing with those who scorn you, as the earth holds up those who dig it, is the highest thing (இகழ்வார்ப் பொறுத்தல் தலை). 579 says the highest quality is to show kindly regard and bear with even those whose nature is to hurt (பொறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பே தலை). Both end on தலை: the forbearance ranked first for a householder is ranked first again in the chapters on kingship.

152 says always bear with excess against you (பொறுத்தல் இறப்பினை என்றும்); Parimelazhagar adds 'even when you are able to punish'. 579 is that case in the ruler, who has the power to punish and is asked to bear with those who harm him. 152 goes a step further than 579 by preferring forgetting the wrong to bearing it.

807 says those whose bond has come by the way of love do not cut off love even when ruinous things are done to them (அழிவந்த செய்யினும் அன்பறார்). 580 says those who want a refinement worth loving will see poison poured and still drink it and stay at ease (பெயக்கண்டும் நஞ்சுண் டமைவர்); Parimelazhagar reads the giver as an intimate. 580 is the extreme instance of the constancy that 807 states in general terms for old friends.

805 advises that when friends do something painful, one should take it as either folly or great intimacy (பேதைமை ஒன்றோ பெருங்கிழமை என்றுணர்க). 580 describes people who drink poison they have seen poured. 805 supplies a way of construing a friend's injury that makes the conduct in 580 intelligible, though 580's own stated motive is the wish for நாகரிகம் and not a charitable reading of the giver.
